title: Farming begins in the Fertile Crescent

facts.text: Warming from 11.7 ka coincides with the earliest farming in the Fertile Crescent, where crop growing and herding opened the Neolithic.
Sheep, goats, cattle and later pigs were domesticated there, along with cereals such as wheat and barley, and legumes.
Barley was domesticated in the Near East around 11,000 years ago, and domesticated emmer wheat appears in Iran by 9,800 BP.
Between 8500 and 7000 BC people in the Fertile Crescent took up the systematic husbandry of plants and animals.
Neolithic settlers had reached Cyprus by 8800–8600 BC.

title: Holocene begins as the Younger Dryas ends

facts.text: The Younger Dryas cold spell, which began about 12,800 years ago, ended about 11,700 years ago, closing the Last Glacial Period and the Pleistocene.
The boundary is a GSSP sample in the NGRIP2 ice core from central Greenland, matched to the end of the Younger Dryas; it was ratified in 2008.
Greenland's average yearly temperature rose by about 8 °C within 40 years, in three steps of five years each.
After this sudden jump, global warming continued at a somewhat gentler pace through the Greenlandian.
Earth has stayed in this interglacial ever since; in the American Southwest the cool, wet pluvial climate gave way to semi-arid conditions.

title: Mammoth steppe gives way to forest and wetland

facts.text: At the start of the Holocene, mossy forests, tundra, lakes and wetlands displaced the vast mammoth steppe.
Higher temperatures and rainfall shrank its habitat, fragmenting animal populations and then driving them extinct.
By about 10,000 years ago patches of closed larch and pine forest had developed in northern Siberia.
As the climate turned warmer and wetter, forests replaced much of the open habitat of the large grazers.
Only from about 10,000 years ago did forbs decline, as woody plants and grasses came to dominate.

title: Pleistocene wolf lineages collapse

facts.text: Ancient wolves lost most of their genetic diversity at the start of the Holocene in Alaska, Siberia and Europe, overlapping little with modern wolves.
In North America a population bottleneck almost erased ancient wolf diversity.
The Japanese wolf turned out to be the last of the Siberian Pleistocene wolves.

title: Baltic Ice Lake gives way to the Yoldia Sea

facts.text: The Baltic Ice Lake ended close to the start of the Holocene.
The Yoldia Sea stage, about 11,700–10,700 years BP, began when the lake fell to sea level and salt water could flow into the basin.
Pine and birch pollen rose sharply around the basin from 11,500 BP, and people lived on its Estonian shores by 11,200–10,200 BP.

conflicts.note: Last Glacial Period page: seawater filled the depressed basin when the ice began melting

title: Megafauna extinctions continue into the Holocene

facts.text: Many megafauna species died out during the Greenlandian, keeping up the extinction rate of the end of the Late Pleistocene.
From the Late Pleistocene into the early Holocene most animals over 45 kg vanished, including 80% of those over a tonne, collapsing faunal density and diversity.
In the Colombian Andes, dung-fungus spores record a second wave of megafaunal extinction around 10,990 BP.
Human activity is blamed for an ongoing mass extinction, the Holocene extinction, that began roughly 10,000 years ago.
Climate change is one main explanation; the balance of human and climatic causes is a long-running controversy, though most scholars accept some human role.

title: Early Holocene sea-level rise

facts.text: Sea level jumped about 60 m in the early Holocene, between about 12,000 and 7,000 years ago.
The rise was fast while continental ice sheets melted, then slowed from over 10 mm a year to under 1 mm a year by 4,200 years ago.
Background rates of about 6–10 mm a year were broken by brief bursts of 30–60 mm a year.
Rising seas drowned vast lowlands and turned parts of continents into islands, cutting off the British Isles, Indonesia, New Guinea and Tasmania.
In Brazil's Bahia region mangroves spread inland as the sea rose.

title: Northern ice sheets melt rapidly

facts.text: The abrupt warming that opened the Holocene, around 9700 BC, set off rapid melting of the remaining ice sheets in North America and Europe.
The Laurentide ice sheet's surface mass balance turned negative only in the early Holocene, once radiative forcing and summer temperatures rose.
In northern British Columbia the Cordilleran ice sheet had essentially melted away by about 11,000 years ago.
Most of the ice-sheet melting and sea-level rise of the last deglaciation came after about 11,000 years ago.
From 8,500 BP, ice pouring from the collapsing Laurentide ice sheet made North Atlantic climate erratic.

title: Meltwater pulse 1B

facts.text: Meltwater pulse 1B is a proposed burst of rapid post-glacial sea-level rise between 11,500 and 11,200 years ago, just after the Younger Dryas.
One study put the rise at 13 m in 300 years, about 40 mm a year; others cut it to 7.5 m or less than 6 m.
Barbados coral cores were read as a 28 m rise in about 500 years around 11,300 years ago.
A peak in Antarctic iceberg discharge about 11,300 years ago, matching the Barbados record, suggests Antarctica contributed significantly.
Some researchers found it was at best a modest speed-up, and at worst no different from steady rise between 11,500 and 10,200 years ago.

contested_note: Its size and even its existence are debated: estimates run from a 28 m rise to no clear departure from steady sea-level rise.

title: Göbekli Tepe built in Upper Mesopotamia

facts.text: Göbekli Tepe, in Upper Mesopotamia in today's Turkey, was built around 9500 BCE and used until about 8000 BCE, at the dawn of the world's first permanent settlements.
Its circular enclosures hold large stone pillars, among the oldest known megaliths, many carved with reliefs of wild animals; the early circles date to c. 9000 BCE.
Its builders were hunter-gatherers who hunted gazelle and ground much cereal; sources differ on whether any of that cereal was domesticated.

title: Green Sahara: the African humid period intensifies

facts.text: Between 11,000 and 10,000 BP, perihelion fell at the June solstice, raising summer sunlight by about 8% and pushing a stronger African monsoon farther north.
From 11,000 years ago a giant Lake Mega-Chad covered more than 350,000 km² of the Chad Basin.
Grasses, trees and lakes covered much of the Sahara; the humid period had begun about 14,600 years ago.
Lake Kivu began overflowing into Lake Tanganyika by about 10,500 BP, and lakes formed in Arabia's Rub' al Khali 9,000–7,000 years ago.
People moved into the greening Sahara: Takarkori was first occupied 10,000–9,000 years ago, and the Kiffian culture flourished 10,000–8,000 years ago.

title: Lake Algonquin floods the upper Great Lakes

facts.text: Glacial Lake Algonquin first flooded about 11,000 years before present.
By then the Laurentide ice front lay along the northern edges of Lakes Superior and Huron.

title: Last notoungulates die out in South America

facts.text: Notoungulata, an order of South American hoofed mammals, lived from about 61 million to 11,000 years ago.
The order included Toxodon, a rhinoceros-sized grazer.

The diversity of the notoungulates declined during the Pliocene and Pleistocene, at the same time as the Great American Interchange let ungulates and other mammals from North America enter South America.
Only the large toxodontids persisted until the end of the Pleistocene, and they perished in the Late Pleistocene megafauna extinctions along with most other large mammals across the Americas.

title: North America loses its ground sloths, horses and short-faced bears

facts.text: Around 11,000 years ago short-faced bears vanished from North America, the last giant ground sloths died out there, and all native horses disappeared.
Shasta ground sloth dung in Arizona's Rampart Cave built up from 13,000 BP and stopped suddenly at 11,000 BP.
Horses had evolved largely in North America; they died out there and were reintroduced only in the 15th century.
Of the continent's odd-toed hoofed mammals, only Baird's tapir, reaching into southern Mexico, survived.
Ground sloths lingered on Caribbean islands until about 4,000 years ago.

title: Wakamiko Caldera eruption in southern Japan

facts.text: Wakamiko Caldera, inside Kyushu's Aira Caldera, produced a VEI 6 eruption of about 12 km³ some time between 9050 and 7050 BCE.

title: Glyptodon and the last glyptodonts die out

facts.text: Glyptodon, a giant plant-eating armadillo relative that had lived in South America since about 3.2 million years ago, died out around 11,000 years ago.
A wetter post-glacial climate replaced C3 grasses with C4 grasses and southern beech, killing off grazing specialists like glyptodonts and toxodonts; human hunting may also have contributed.
Its relatives Doedicurus and Panochthus survived on the Argentine Pampas into the early Holocene, living alongside people for at least 4,000 years.

title: First livestock domesticated in the Fertile Crescent

facts.text: Zooarchaeology shows that goats, pigs, sheep and taurine cattle were the first livestock, domesticated in the Fertile Crescent 11,000–10,000 years ago.
The earliest dates in northern Mesopotamia are c. 9000 BCE for goats and sheep, c. 8500 BCE for pigs and c. 8000 BCE for cattle.
The milder climate after the Younger Dryas set the stage; by 10,000 years ago hunters were culling young males and sparing females to breed.
Domestication began a rapid shift in the evolution, ecology and demography of people and of many animal and plant species.
In Eurasia domestic animals then overtook other primates as the main source of new human infections.

title: Ancylus Lake fills the Baltic basin

facts.text: After the Yoldia Sea, post-glacial uplift turned the Baltic basin into the freshwater Ancylus Lake, from about 10,700 to 9,800 years BP.
Its expansion forced people on the former Yoldia shore near Pärnu to retreat inland.
The lake drained to the sea through the Dana River between 10,200 and 9,800 BP, and salt water began entering at 9,800 BP.

title: Last mainland woolly mammoths die out

facts.text: Woolly mammoths survived in mainland Siberia until around 10,000 years ago; a small population lived on Wrangel Island much longer.
The youngest European mammoth remains come from the Southern Urals, 9650 BCE, and Cherepovets in Russia, 9290–9180 BCE.
In Eurasia, cold-adapted giants such as the woolly mammoth and woolly rhinoceros were generally the last of the megafauna to go, around 10,000 BP.
The youngest mainland fossils come from Siberia's Kyttyk Peninsula and are 9,650 years old.
Trackways at St. Mary Reservoir in Canada show a mammoth herd of adults, subadults and young still roaming there 11,300–11,000 years ago.

title: Modern coyote appears

facts.text: The modern coyote appeared around 10,000 years ago, most likely descended from the Pleistocene coyote.
By the Early Pleistocene, 1 million years ago, Canis latrans, the coyote, was already in existence.

title: Last woolly rhinoceroses

facts.text: The youngest woolly rhinoceros bones, from the Southern Urals, date to 9450 BCE.
Its DNA was last detected in permafrost near Russia's Kolyma River dated to 8050–7650 BCE.
Its extinction was part of the end-Pleistocene event that wiped out most large land animals, after its range had shrunk toward Siberia from 17,000 years ago.

title: Doggerland drowns beneath the North Sea

facts.text: In the early Holocene, Doggerland linked eastern Britain to northern France, the Low Countries, north-west Germany and Jutland.
By 9000 BCE a large tidal bay had formed between eastern England and Dogger Bank, and rapid sea-level rise followed.
Between 10,000 and 7,000 years ago rising seas broke Doggerland into low islands and then submerged it completely.
Dogger Bank became an island, and Britain was finally cut off from the European mainland around 6500 BCE.
Most evidence of people living there dates to the Mesolithic of the early Holocene.

title: Domestication spreads beyond the Fertile Crescent

facts.text: Between 10,000 and 7,000 BP plants and animals were rapidly domesticated in tropical and subtropical Asia, Africa and Central America.
Drainage ditches at Kuk Swamp in highland New Guinea show taro and other crops cultivated by about 11,000 BP, perhaps by 8000 BCE.
The Near East was not the only cradle of farming: maize was domesticated in Mesoamerica from about 7000 BCE, and rice in the Far East.
Mehrgarh in Balochistan, South Asia's earliest Neolithic site with wheat, barley and herding, is dated variously from 8500 to 6500 BCE.
Cereal farming and herding reached the eastern Sahara by about 7000 BC.

title: Bering land bridge floods

facts.text: Around 8000 BCE rising seas flooded the Beringian land bridge, closing the main migration route from Siberia.
The drowning formed the Bering Strait and separated Asia from the Americas.
Estimates from Bering Strait depths and the global sea-level curve alone put the final drowning around 11,000 years BP.

title: Fennoscandian ice sheet melts away

facts.text: The Scandinavian ice sheet withdrew into the mountains, leaving Russia by 10.6 ka and Finland by 10.1 ka.
Its southern Norway centre vanished about a thousand years after 10.1 ka.
By 9.7 ka the last remnant of the Fennoscandian ice sheet lay in the eastern Sarek Mountains.

title: Holocene Climatic Optimum begins

facts.text: The Holocene Climatic Optimum was a warm period lasting roughly from 9,500 to 5,500 years BP.
Northern Hemisphere heating peaked about 9,000 years ago, when axial tilt was 24° and perihelion fell in northern summer.
In New Zealand and Antarctica the warmest stretch, often called the Early Holocene Climatic Optimum, came earlier, roughly 10,500 to 8,000 years ago.
The Amery Ice Shelf in Antarctica retreated about 80 km landward during that southern warm interval.
North-western North America peaked 11,000–9,000 years ago while the Laurentide ice sheet still chilled eastern Canada.

title: Sapropel S1 forms in the eastern Mediterranean

facts.text: The latest eastern Mediterranean sapropel, a dark, organic-rich mud laid down when bottom waters lose oxygen, formed between 9,500 and 5,500 years ago.
This S1 layer is tied to the African humid period: greater Nile and other river discharge freshened the sea, stratifying it and making it eutrophic.
Sapropels recur about every 21,000 years, following Earth's orbital cycles; when Nile discharge fell, deposition off its delta stopped.

title: Post-glacial rebound lifts Scandinavia and Canada

facts.text: Freed of ice, Scandinavia rose 9–13 mm a year between 9,500 and 5,000 years ago.
The isostatic movements triggered large earthquakes in Scandinavia about 9,000 years ago, forming postglacial faults.
Hudson Bay, the Great Lakes and Fennoscandia are still rebounding; in Canada the rising land drained the Champlain Sea by about 10,000 years ago.

title: Last sabre-toothed Smilodon

facts.text: The youngest remains of the North American Smilodon fatalis, which ranged from Alberta to north-western South America, date to 7615–7305 BCE.
The South American Smilodon populator survived a little longer; its youngest remains, at Itapipoca in Brazil, date to 7129–6239 BCE.
With them the last Smilodon species died out.

title: Last American mastodons

facts.text: The youngest remains of the American mastodon date to 7110–6810 BCE.
Mastodons, mammoths and horses roamed North America as recently as 10,000 years ago; in Minnesota the giant animals were gone by about 9,000 years ago.

title: Modern Great Barrier Reef begins to grow

facts.text: The present living Great Barrier Reef is believed to have begun growing on an older platform about 9,000 years ago.
The Great Barrier Reef is the world's largest coral reef system, made of over 2,900 individual reefs and 900 islands stretching over 2,300 kilometres across about 344,400 square kilometres.
The land under the current reef was a coastal plain formed from eroded sediments of the Great Dividing Range, with some larger hills that were mostly remnants of older reefs or, rarely, volcanoes.

title: Pluvial Lake Lahontan dries up

facts.text: Lake Lahontan in the Great Basin had largely disappeared in its extended form by about 9,000 years ago.
Further south, tufa at Lake Cahuilla records a wet period that ended 9,000 years before present.

title: Proposed Black Sea deluge

facts.text: A catastrophic inflow of Mediterranean seawater is proposed to have flooded the Black Sea, then a freshwater lake.
The flood was first dated to about 7,600 years ago, then redated in 2003 to 8,800 years ago, c. 6800 BCE.
The hypothesis is controversial; other authors argue for a gradual inundation of the basin.
Opponents cite water flowing out of the basin as late as 15,000 years ago and sill sediments building up from before 10,000 years ago.

contested_note: The flood is controversial: dated c. 7,600 then c. 8,800 years ago, and many authors favour a gradual inundation instead.

conflicts.note: Original 1997 date (Northgrippian)

title: Kurile Lake caldera eruption in Kamchatka

facts.text: In 6460–6414 BCE a very large eruption formed the present Kurile Lake caldera and its ignimbrite, dropping ash up to 1,700 km away.
Rated VEI 7, it produced about 155 km³ of material.
Two sulfate spikes in Greenland's GISP2 ice core, around 6470 and 6476 BC, may record it.
It ranks with Fisher, Kikai and Mazama among the largest eruptions around the Pacific Ring of Fire, during an especially active spell in 6600–6400 BCE.
